abstract: Humans spontaneously move together to rhythm, yet how the body organizes its movements is poorly understood and determining which aspects of this organization support interpersonal coordination requires state-of-the-art analysis methods. By applying for the first time Frequency-resolved Network Estimation via Source Separation (FREQ-NESS) to movement data, we reveal a rhythmic architecture of human movement and show how it shapes coordination between individuals. Using full-body motion capture from dancing dyads, we identify a small set of frequency-specific bodily networks whose organization follows a harmonic hierarchy centred on the musical beat. These networks exhibit distinct spatial configurations, revealing how different rhythmic timescales recruit different patterns of bodily movement. Crucially, not all rhythmic networks contribute equally to interpersonal coordination. The beat emerges as a prominent timescale at which bodily organization and social coordination converge. Shared music primarily enhances the temporal alignment of movement dynamics, whereas visual contact additionally promotes similarity in the bodily configurations expressed by partners, with particularly clear effects at the beat. Together, these findings suggest that interpersonal coordination does not arise from rhythmic movement indiscriminately, but from the engagement of specific rhythmic modes within a structured bodily system. By linking the organization of individual movement to coordination between people, our findings establish a framework for understanding how rhythm connects bodily dynamics and social interaction.
